transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello. Um... well, I guess I'm here because I've been having some trouble at work lately. I'm an auditor, and... I don't know. What pushed me to finally make an appointment is that I just keep starting follow-up items after audits, or mentorship events. I have every intention of finishing them when I start. But then... I'll find out days later that the final email, or a review note, or a form just... never actually got done. So... yeah. That's why I'm here.
Over the past few weeks, how has your mood been? Have you been feeling sad, down, or empty most of the time?
Um... no. Not really. I mean, my mood is fine, I guess. I'm just... frustrated with the work stuff. But I wouldn't say I feel sad or empty. Just normal.
When you're working on tasks that require you to focus, like reading through audit documents or reviewing reports, do you find it hard to concentrate or do your thoughts wander easily?

Yeah... I suppose so. If I'm trying to review an audit file, it doesn't take much. Like a Slack ping, or... someone talking outside my office. Even just, um, a thought about my marathon training. It just... pulls me completely off track.
Do you find yourself fidgeting, tapping your fingers or feet, or having trouble sitting still, even when you're trying to focus on work?

Um... yeah, I guess. When I'm in meetings, I usually tap my foot under the table... or click my pen. I guess I shift around in the chair a lot, too. My colleague actually joked recently that she can hear my leg going. So... yes.
When did you first notice these difficulties with concentration and fidgeting? Were you like this as a child or teenager, or did this start more recently as an adult?

Um... I suppose it's always been there. Even when I was a kid... elementary school, maybe. My report cards always said things like... I was smart but I lost assignments a lot. Or I'd rush and miss details. 

I guess I talked out of turn, too. And... I always needed reminders to actually finish things. My mom still brings it up sometimes. She jokes that I could get a perfect score on a test but completely forget to turn in the project that was sitting right there in my backpack. So... yeah, it's not new.
When you were younger, did teachers or your parents ever describe you as hyperactive, overly energetic, or say that you were 'always on the go' or 'driven by a motor'?

I guess so. Um... yeah, probably. It's... it's still like that, honestly. Like on weekends... I'll tell my husband I'm just going to rest. But then I... I don't know, I just bounce around. I'll go from doing laundry to checking emails, then... go for a run, or work on volunteer planning. I don't really stop until I'm exhausted. So... yeah, I suppose 'always on the go' fits.

Beyond the work situation you mentioned, how much do these difficulties with focus, organization, and staying on task affect other areas of your life—like your relationships with your husband, your volunteer work, or managing things at home?

Um... I suppose it affects things a fair amount. 

Like at work... I know you asked about other areas, but... the mistakes and the unfinished follow-ups, they actually affected a client review recently. I'm... well, I'm worried people are questioning if I can even handle the promotion I'm up for. It's... not great. 

And at home... um... my husband just handles the bills now. And other commitments I said I'd take care of. He had to take them over because... well, he can't really count on me to finish them reliably. So... he just does it. Yeah.
When you think back to elementary school—say, around age 7 or 8—were you already having these kinds of problems with attention, organization, and finishing tasks, or did they develop later?

Um... yeah. Like I mentioned earlier, it was already happening back then. Around seven or eight, I guess. 

That's when those report cards started. The ones where teachers said I was bright but... kept losing my assignments, or rushing and missing small details. And talking out of turn. I always needed reminders. And... like I said about my mom joking about the backpack thing... acing the test but forgetting to turn in the actual project. 

So... yes. It didn't just develop later. It was there in elementary school.

You mentioned the work mistakes affected a client review and your husband had to take over bill payments. Looking back to when you were in school—did these attention and organization problems cause similar kinds of trouble for you academically or socially back then?

Um... I don't really know. I mean, I guess I got in trouble for talking sometimes, or... forgetting things. But I still got decent grades eventually, so... I don't think it was a huge issue. I just... kind of got through it.

By the time you were around 12 years old, were these problems with attention, finishing tasks, and fidgeting already causing you real trouble—like affecting your grades, getting you in trouble at school, or causing problems with friends?

Um... I don't really remember it causing... real trouble, I guess. 

I mean, I mentioned the report cards and the talking, but... I don't know if it was actually causing problems with friends or... anything like that by the time I was twelve. I just... I don't recall it being a major issue. I was just... going to school.

Looking back at your school years—by age 12, were there times when your teachers or parents felt these attention or organization problems were actually getting in the way of your schoolwork, or causing enough trouble that they were concerned about it?

Um... yeah, I mean... I think I already said this. The teachers were definitely noticing it. 

They'd write on my report cards that I was... bright, but I was losing assignments and missing details because I was rushing. And... talking out of turn. They were always having to remind me to finish my work. And my mom... she still brings up how I would do fine on a test but completely forget to hand in a project because it was just sitting in my backpack. So... yeah, they were concerned, I guess.

When you were around 12 years old, did your teachers or parents ever sit down with you or talk to your parents about these attention or organization problems? Did anyone ever try to help you with it, or were you sent to see a counselor or doctor about it?

Um... no, not that I can remember. 

I mean... nobody sent me to a doctor or a counselor for it back then. They just... told me to try harder, I guess. I don't remember any big sit-down meetings about it. It was just... comments on report cards. That's about it.

When you were around 12 years old, did these problems with attention and organization actually affect your grades or cause you to fall behind in school, or did they keep you from doing things you wanted to do?
Um... no, not really. I mean, my grades were okay. I passed everything. I don't think it stopped me from doing anything I wanted to do. It was just... normal school stuff, I guess. I got by fine.

You mentioned your grades were okay and you got by fine in school. But thinking back to around age 12—did these attention problems, the rushing, losing assignments, or needing reminders actually make things harder for you compared to other kids your age? Like, were you falling behind them, or did you have to work much harder than they did to keep up?

I don't know... I guess I didn't really compare myself to other kids. I just did my work. I mean, maybe I had to spend a little more time finding my stuff, but... I don't think it was that big of a deal. I kept up fine.

When you were around 12 years old, did you ever get in trouble at school—like detention, being sent to the principal's office, or losing privileges—because of the attention problems, rushing, or talking out of turn?
Um... no. Not that I recall. I wasn't really a troublemaker. I mean, maybe a teacher told me to quiet down once in a while, but... no detentions or anything like that.

When you were around 12 years old, thinking about things like getting homework done, organizing your schoolwork, or managing your time—did you find that you had to put in noticeably more effort than other kids to stay on top of things, or did you struggle with any of that in a way that was frustrating or difficult for you?
I don't know... I didn't really pay attention to how hard other kids were working. I just did what I had to do. I don't remember it being... frustrating, really. It was just homework.

When you were around 12 years old, did your parents or teachers ever express worry that your attention problems or disorganization might affect your future—like your ability to succeed in school or get into a good program?
No... I don't think so. I don't remember anyone ever saying anything like that to me. They just... expected me to do my work, I guess. That's about it.

When you were around 12 years old, even though your grades were okay, did these attention problems—like losing assignments, rushing, or needing reminders—actually make it harder for you to get things done at home or school compared to what was expected of you?

I guess... yeah. I mean, even back in elementary school, my report cards usually said I was bright, but... they also said I lost assignments, or rushed past small details. Sometimes that I talked out of turn and needed reminders to finish things. 

My mother actually still jokes about it. She says I could ace a test but completely forget the project sitting right in my backpack. So... I suppose it was a little harder, yes.

patient.answer: No... I don't think so. I don't remember anyone ever saying anything like that to me. They just... expected me to do my work, I guess. That's about it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's childhood ADHD symptoms caused clinically significant impairment in functioning by age 12, which is required for ADHD diagnosis. doctor.question: When you were around 12 years old, even though your grades were okay, did these attention problems—like losing assignments, rushing, or needing reminders—actually make it harder for you to get things done at home or school compared to what was expected of you?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even in elementary school, my report cards said I was bright but lost assignments, rushed past small details, talked out of turn, and needed reminders to finish work. My mother still jokes that I could ace a test but forget the project sitting in my backpack.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether the attention problems (losing assignments, rushing, needing reminders) made it harder to get things done at home or school when the patient was around 12 years old, which directly relates to the onset of symptoms prior to age 12 (additional_requirement_1).

patient.answer:
I guess... yeah. I mean, even back in elementary school, my report cards usually said I was bright, but... they also said I lost assignments, or rushed past small details. Sometimes that I talked out of turn and needed reminders to finish things. 

My mother actually still jokes about it. She says I could ace a test but completely forget the project sitting right in my backpack. So... I suppose it was a little harder, yes.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong pattern of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that began in childhood (elementary school, age 7-8) and persists into adulthood. Core ADHD symptoms are well-documented: difficulty sustaining attention (easily distracted by Slack, conversations, thoughts), hyperactivity (fidgeting, foot-tapping, pen-clicking, restlessness, constant activity), and executive dysfunction (losing assignments, incomplete follow-ups, poor task completion). Functional impairment is evident in both current work performance (client review affected, promotion concerns, reliance on spouse for bill management) and childhood (teacher-noted assignment loss, rushing errors, talking out of turn, requiring reminders). The symptom onset clearly precedes age 12, and symptoms have persisted across multiple life domains and decades. No alternative diagnosis (mood disorder, anxiety disorder, substance use) accounts for the presentation. The patient meets DSM-5 criteria for ADHD, combined presentation.
